distillation_scope_note: Pure disease/syndrome-name distillation: Febrile neutropenia. Malignancy, chemotherapy, transplant, congenital/drug-induced neutropenia, steroid exposure, catheters, prophylaxis, resistance, and local epidemiology are represented only as risk or treatment-context modifiers.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Quantitative and functional neutrophil defense failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe reduction in circulating neutrophils and impaired phagocyte function reduces bacterial and fungal containment, blunts pus formation and localizing signs, and allows rapid dissemination from small portals of entry.
Cumulative exposure to ANC below 0.5 x10^9/L, especially below 0.1 x10^9/L for more than 7 days, shifts risk toward resistant bacteria, invasive molds, enterocolitis, pneumonia, and higher mortality.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Mucosal barrier injury and gut translocation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Oropharyngeal and gastrointestinal epithelial injury permits viridans streptococci, Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas, anaerobes, Candida, and mixed flora to enter tissue and blood; severe bowel involvement may become neutropenic enterocolitis.

Central venous catheters, ports, dialysis catheters, and parenteral nutrition lines provide biofilm-protected entry for coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, gram-negative rods, and Candida.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Occult bacterial tissue or bloodstream burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable bacterial burden from gut, catheter, lung, urinary tract, skin, perianal tissue, or another source. Because neutrophils are absent, fever may be the only early sign before bacteremia, pneumonia, typhlitis, or shock emerges.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pseudomonal and high-risk gram-negative invasive activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pseudomonas and other rapidly progressive gram-negative pathogens can cause bacteremia, ecthyma gangrenosum, perianal necrosis, pneumonia, vasodilatory shock, DIC physiology, AKI, and ARDS in profoundly neutropenic hosts.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Gram-positive device or mucosal bloodstream activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Biofilm or mucositis-associated gram-positive bloodstream activity, including coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, and viridans streptococci. This mechanism determines when anti-MRSA or anti-resistant gram-positive coverage has causal value.

Candida or mold invasion during persistent or prolonged neutropenia, often after broad antibacterial exposure or antifungal prophylaxis; may present as persistent fever, pulmonary nodules or halo lesions, candidemia, hepatosplenic lesions, ocular seeding, or disseminated disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Undrained focus or retained infected device
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: An infected catheter, necrotic perianal lesion, typhlitis with necrosis, abscess, obstructed urinary tract, or infected thrombus sustains pathogen burden despite active drugs.

Profound neutropenia, corticosteroids, lymphocyte depletion, transplant immunosuppression, infancy, or frailty can lower fever amplitude, CRP/WBC response, local tenderness, pulmonary infiltrate visibility, and pus formation even when invasive infection is present.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Septic organ dysfunction under neutropenic host defense failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Vasoplegia, capillary leak, tissue hypoperfusion, microvascular injury, and inflammatory-coagulation crosstalk produce shock, lactatemia, AKI, ARDS, DIC physiology, encephalopathy, and death risk.

Recovery of granulopoiesis improves microbial clearance but can transiently unmask inflammatory lesions, fever, pulmonary infiltrates, enterocolitis pain, and immune-reconstitution-like tissue inflammation.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Febrile neutropenia is anchored by low ANC or expected imminent severe ANC decline.
Most episodes have leukopenia, although leukemia blasts, steroids, or marrow recovery can dissociate WBC from ANC.
Duration-depth burden is measured by days of clinically important neutropenia.
Mold and Candida hazards rise as neutropenia persists despite antibacterial therapy.
Low neutrophil reserve permits rapid bacterial expansion from small inocula.
Mucosal injury is the observed clinical state that exposes translocation portals.
Oropharyngeal mucosal damage is a common visible manifestation and raises viridans/Candida risk.
Barrier breakdown allows gastrointestinal and oral organisms to enter tissue and blood.
Gut mucosal injury plus neutropenia produces typhlitis in a subset.
CT or ultrasound bowel wall thickening is a core objective sign of neutropenic enterocolitis.
The presence of intravascular material is the exposure axis for biofilm-associated infection.
Biofilm seeding increases the probability that the catheter is the fever source.
Catheter biofilms commonly seed gram-positive bloodstream infection in neutropenic hosts.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Fever amplitude may be low or absent with corticosteroids, profound immunosuppression, infancy, frailty, or septic shock hypothermia.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Fever is the usual presenting signal when neutrophils are too low to generate local signs.
Reported fever, chills, or recurrent fever often supplies the key presentation evidence.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: CRP can be delayed or modest under immunosuppression but is often elevated.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-6 acute-phase signaling raises CRP during bacterial or fungal FN.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: More informative for bacterial sepsis than localized mucositis or pure fungal breakthrough.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacterial systemic infection commonly raises procalcitonin, especially gram-negative sepsis.
Bloodstream pathogen burden drives positive cultures, although cultures are confirmatory context rather than the only ranking evidence.
Pseudomonal activity is encoded as a treatment-context risk axis for antipseudomonal coverage.
Ecthyma gangrenosum is a sentinel skin sign of invasive Pseudomonas, especially in neutropenic patients.
Perianal cellulitis, necrosis, or abscess can be an occult source in neutropenic fever.
High-risk gram-negative burden is the direct causal driver of neutropenic sepsis hazard.
Line infection, severe mucositis, skin focus, pneumonia, shock, or known MRSA/VRE context increases gram-positive coverage value.
Persistent fever after antibacterial exposure and prolonged neutropenia raises invasive fungal probability.
Fungal breakthrough often appears as pulmonary infiltrates or nodules; infiltrates may be minimal until neutrophil recovery.
Nodular lung lesions, sometimes with halo sign or cavitation, suggest invasive mold disease.
Breakthrough fungal activity creates a major event hazard when fever persists despite antibacterial therapy.
Retained device, necrotic bowel, perianal necrosis, or abscess creates a need for removal, drainage, or debridement.
Failure is represented by low adequacy until the source is removed or drained.
Uncontrolled source continues to seed pathogen burden despite systemic therapy.
Immunosuppression or steroids may lower fever amplitude even with invasive infection.
Absence of pus, mild pain, or normal early imaging does not exclude severe infection under neutropenia.
Fever, shock, hypovolemia, anemia, and cytokine response produce tachycardia.
Tachypnea tracks sepsis, metabolic acidosis, pneumonia, or early respiratory failure.
Vasoplegia and capillary leak reduce MAP.
Hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction elevate lactate.
Shock, nephrotoxins, and renal hypoperfusion produce AKI.
Organ dysfunction creates daily AKI event hazard.
Sepsis, pneumonia, transfusion burden, and inflammatory recovery can precipitate ARDS.
Severe gram-negative or fungal sepsis can trigger consumptive coagulopathy.
Mortality hazard emerges from shock, delayed active coverage, fungal breakthrough, organ failure, source failure, and host reserve.
Rising ANC is captured by recovery activity.
Neutrophil recovery moves ANC back toward baseline.

axes.shape_free_text: Single fever spike or sustained fever is typical, but amplitude can be blunted by corticosteroids, profound immunosuppression, infancy, frailty, or late septic shock.
Reported fever, recurrent fever, chills, or rigor when exact temperature is unavailable.
Core measurement. High-risk FN usually has ANC <0.5, and profound risk is strongest below 0.1; ANC may be expected to fall below 0.5 even if not yet at nadir.
Usually low during marrow suppression; can be dissociated from ANC in leukemia, steroid exposure, G-CSF effect, or marrow recovery.
Observed or expected duration of ANC below clinically important thresholds; prolonged duration shifts toward mold, Candida, typhlitis, and resistant infection hazards.
Rising ANC or marrow recovery state; reduces bacterial clearance failure but may unmask inflammatory foci.
Degree to which local signs are muted: little pus, weak tenderness, small infiltrates, or sparse exam findings despite invasive infection.
Often elevated in FN infection but may lag or be attenuated in heavily immunosuppressed patients.
Higher in bacterial sepsis, especially gram-negative disease; may be modest in localized mucositis or invasive fungal disease.
Tachycardia tracks fever, sepsis, pain, dehydration, anemia, and shock.
Tachypnea may be the first organ dysfunction sign and can occur with pneumonia, metabolic acidosis, shock, or ARDS.
Falls with vasoplegia, capillary leak, dehydration, bleeding, or septic shock.
Low MAP indicates sepsis-induced hypoperfusion and drives resuscitation and vasopressor effect.
Can be normal early; declines with pneumonia, fungal lung disease, ARDS, fluid overload, or shock.
Rises with septic shock, tissue hypoperfusion, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
Rises with AKI from shock, nephrotoxic antimicrobials, tumor lysis overlap, or baseline kidney disease.
Rises with prerenal azotemia, AKI, catabolism, bleeding, or kidney reserve limits.
Often low from marrow suppression or chemotherapy; sharp fall can indicate sepsis-associated DIC or bleeding risk.
Rises with sepsis-associated coagulation activation, thrombosis, DIC, or malignancy background.
Can rise with septic cholestasis, hepatic toxicity, biliary source, hemolysis, or underlying malignancy therapy.
May rise with sepsis-associated hepatic injury, antifungals, chemotherapy, viral reactivation, or shock liver.
Composite mucosal injury in oral, esophageal, intestinal, or perianal surfaces; raises translocation and candidemia risk.
Oral mucositis grade; grade 3-4 increases viridans streptococci, Candida, bacteremia, pain, and reduced oral intake.
Diarrhea may occur with enterocolitis, chemotherapy mucosal injury, C. difficile, or graft-versus-host disease context.
Abdominal pain is important for typhlitis, appendicitis, cholecystitis, pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, or bowel perforation in FN.
Ileocecal or right-sided abdominal pain localizes toward neutropenic enterocolitis but can be blunted.
Measured bowel wall thickness on CT/ultrasound; >4 mm over a sufficient segment supports neutropenic enterocolitis, and larger thickness correlates with severity.
Clinical-imaging presence of typhlitis/neutropenic enterocolitis; not a separate first-layer leaf here but an event/focus inside FN.
Perianal cellulitis, ulceration, abscess, necrosis, or pain; important occult focus in neutropenic fever.
Violaceous plaque, bulla, eschar, or necrotic ulcer suspicious for ecthyma gangrenosum, strongly linked to invasive Pseudomonas in neutropenia.
Extent of radiographic infiltrates from bacterial pneumonia, fungal pneumonia, PJP, viral infection, hemorrhage, or ARDS overlap.
Pulmonary nodules, halo-sign nodules, or focal masslike lesions in persistent FN suggest invasive mold or septic embolic disease.
Cavitary nodules can appear with invasive mold infection, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus aureus, Nocardia, or septic emboli in neutropenic hosts.
Central line, port, Hickman, PICC, dialysis catheter, or other intravascular access present.
Probability a central line or intravascular device is the fever or bloodstream infection source.
Probability lung is the dominant source: bacterial pneumonia, fungal pneumonia, PJP, viral pneumonia, or mixed infection.
Probability gut, biliary, urinary, or intra-abdominal focus is the source; includes typhlitis and abscess context.
Probability perianal tissue is the actionable source requiring exam, imaging, antibiotics, drainage, debridement, or diversion.
Probability that a drainable/removable focus exists: catheter, abscess, necrotic tissue, obstructed system, or bowel complication.
Need for catheter removal, drainage, debridement, bowel rest/surgery, urinary decompression, or other focus control.
Adequacy of achieved source control; low values sustain fever and pathogen burden even under active antimicrobial exposure.
Probability blood cultures are positive. This is confirmatory/context evidence and should not be the only ordinary diagnostic evidence.
Probability current antibacterial regimen covers the true bacterial pathogen; depends on source, local ecology, prior prophylaxis, cultures, and susceptibilities.
Probability current antifungal regimen covers the true fungal pathogen and reaches the affected compartment.
Risk context that Pseudomonas is the causative pathogen: profound neutropenia, prior broad antibiotics, hospital exposure, ecthyma gangrenosum, perianal lesion, pneumonia, or shock.
ESBL, AmpC, CRE, resistant Pseudomonas, or other MDR gram-negative risk from prior colonization, recent broad antibiotics, local ecology, or healthcare exposure.
MRSA, resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci, ampicillin-resistant Enterococcus, or viridans severe mucositis context requiring gram-positive coverage.
Persistent fever, prolonged neutropenia, mold-active prophylaxis failure, Candida risk, pulmonary nodules, sinus findings, or hepatosplenic lesions increasing antifungal escalation value.
Immediate allergy/anaphylaxis context that constrains antipseudomonal beta-lactams and may require allergy assessment, graded challenge, desensitization, or alternative combinations.
Renal reserve constraint affecting beta-lactam, vancomycin, aminoglycoside, amphotericin, acyclovir, and TMP-SMX dosing and toxicity.
Hepatic reserve and drug-toxicity context for azoles, chemotherapy, parenteral nutrition, and sepsis-associated cholestasis.
QT or drug-interaction constraint relevant to fluoroquinolones, azoles, antiemetics, antipsychotics, and electrolyte derangements.
Confidence that pathogen identity and susceptibility are known enough to narrow therapy while maintaining active coverage.
Hemodynamic stability, defervescence trend, source control, and improving labs that permit narrowing or stopping redundant agents.
Hazard of secondary bacterial, fungal, viral, or C. difficile infection from broad antimicrobials, devices, ICU care, mucositis, and immunosuppression.
Daily hazard of typhlitis, bowel necrosis, perforation, hemorrhage, or need for colectomy under mucosal injury plus neutropenia.
Daily hazard of gram-negative bacteremia/sepsis, including Pseudomonas and resistant Enterobacterales.
Daily hazard of Candida or mold breakthrough infection during persistent fever or prolonged neutropenia.
Daily hazard of bacterial, fungal, viral, PJP, or mixed pneumonia during FN.
Daily hazard of perianal cellulitis, abscess, necrosis, ecthyma gangrenosum, or need for debridement/diversion.
Daily hazard of progression to septic shock; rises with gram-negative burden, delayed active coverage, source failure, high lactate, and low MAP.
Daily AKI hazard from shock, nephrotoxic antimicrobials, contrast, tumor lysis overlap, dehydration, or baseline kidney disease.
Daily ARDS or severe hypoxemic respiratory failure hazard from sepsis, pneumonia, fungal disease, transfusion burden, or inflammatory recovery.
Daily DIC hazard from severe gram-negative sepsis, fungal sepsis, shock, leukemia/APL overlap, or massive tissue injury.

Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from septic shock, delayed active coverage, source control failure, invasive fungal breakthrough, pneumonia, typhlitis, perianal necrosis, AKI, ARDS, DIC, underlying host reserve, and neutropenia duration.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Strongest when ANC is below 0.5 x10^9/L and especially below 0.1 x10^9/L.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Lower ANC weakens bacterial containment and raises sepsis hazard.
Fungal breakthrough risk rises with persistent fever and prolonged neutropenia.
Barrier injury plus neutropenia is the causal substrate for typhlitis.
Greater bowel wall thickening correlates with severe enterocolitis and complication risk.
Intravascular access is required for catheter-source probability to become high.
Likely catheter infection creates a source-control requirement for line removal or exchange.
Perianal lesions in neutropenia can progress rapidly to necrosis and septic shock.
Ecthyma gangrenosum strongly increases the probability of invasive Pseudomonas.

axis_couplings.conditionality: If current regimen lacks antipseudomonal activity or local resistance is high.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Pseudomonas context makes non-antipseudomonal regimens inactive.
Active coverage rapidly lowers viable bacterial burden and sepsis hazard.
MDR risk reduces the probability that narrow empiric regimens are active.
Persistent fever and pulmonary or Candida context raises fungal event hazard.
Compartment-active antifungal therapy lowers fungal progression hazard.
Greater lung involvement raises ARDS and ventilatory support hazard.
Low MAP is shock physiology and predicts escalating shock hazard.
Lactate elevation marks tissue hypoperfusion and shock risk.
Septic shock promotes AKI through hypoperfusion and nephrotoxic exposure.
Shock is a dominant driver of early FN mortality.
AKI worsens drug dosing, fluid balance, and organ-failure mortality.
ARDS and mechanical ventilation hazard increase mortality in neutropenic sepsis.
DIC increases bleeding, thrombosis, organ failure, and mortality hazard.
Adequate source control lowers ongoing burden and mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefepime has antipseudomonal activity when the isolate is susceptible.
ESBL, AmpC, CRE, or resistant Pseudomonas can defeat cefepime.
Immediate beta-lactam allergy may require allergy evaluation, alternative therapy, or desensitization.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad-spectrum antibacterial pressure can select secondary infection or C. difficile.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid empiric bacterial vector for high-risk FN when broad antipseudomonal beta-lactam activity is needed and MDR risk does not mandate carbapenem-level coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anaerobic and gut-flora coverage is useful when typhlitis or intra-abdominal source is likely.
ESBL, AmpC, CRE, or resistant Pseudomonas can make this regimen inactive.

side_effects.interpretation: AKI signal is higher when combined with vancomycin or baseline renal dysfunction.
Broad anaerobic and gram-negative pressure can select secondary infection.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid empiric bacterial vector when gut, oral, perianal, or polymicrobial source context is plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbapenem coverage is more reliable for ESBL and some high-inoculum resistant gram-negative contexts.
Meropenem provides antipseudomonal activity when susceptible.

side_effects.interpretation: Carbapenem pressure selects resistant organisms, Candida overgrowth, and C. difficile risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad empiric or targeted bacterial vector when MDR gram-negative, ESBL, severe shock, or high-inoculum intra-abdominal context makes narrower coverage fragile.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Catheter-related gram-positive bacteremia is a common value context for vancomycin.
MRSA or resistant coagulase-negative staphylococcal risk raises vancomycin value.
AUC-guided dosing and renal monitoring are required; toxicity is amplified with other nephrotoxins.

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin nephrotoxicity, especially with piperacillin-tazobactam or baseline kidney injury.
Nephrotoxicity enters outcome through AKI hazard.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add-on gram-positive vector for line infection, skin/soft tissue focus, pneumonia, hemodynamic instability, or resistant gram-positive context; stopping emerges when culture and stability axes no longer support it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent fever, pulmonary nodules, candidemia, or prolonged neutropenia shifts value toward antifungal escalation.
Drug class must match suspected Candida, mold, resistant yeast, and tissue compartment.
Liposomal amphotericin and some adjuncts carry renal toxicity.
Azoles and echinocandins require hepatic monitoring and interaction review.

side_effects.interpretation: Azole or echinocandin hepatic enzyme elevation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Antifungal vector for persistent or high-risk FN where fungal probability or documented Candida/mold disease is high; exact agent is selected by suspected pathogen, prophylaxis, compartment, and toxicity axes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: G-CSF value is highest when marrow can recover and neutropenia is profound or expected to be prolonged.
Rapid neutrophil recovery can rarely worsen lung inflammation in severe pneumonia or ARDS context.

side_effects.interpretation: Cytokine-mediated fever or bone pain can mimic persistent infection.
Inflammatory lung worsening is uncommon but relevant in severe pneumonia or ARDS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Host-defense recovery vector for high-risk or complicated FN; it does not replace active antimicrobials or source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Procedural source control has value only when a removable, drainable, or debrideable focus exists.
Catheter removal can rapidly stop biofilm seeding.
Necrotic perianal tissue or abscess may require debridement, drainage, or diversion.

side_effects.interpretation: Contrast, surgery, and hemodynamic stress can contribute to AKI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical vector for retained lines, necrotic tissue, typhlitis complications, abscess, obstruction, or infected thrombus.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Known pathogen and susceptibility permit narrowing without losing active coverage.
Stability and source control lower the risk of narrowing.
Persistent profound neutropenia may require continued broad protection until risk falls.

secondary_infection_hazard.clinical_rationale: Narrowing redundant therapy reduces antimicrobial pressure and secondary infection hazard.

active_antibiotic_coverage_probability.clinical_rationale: Coverage should remain microbiologically active when narrowing is appropriate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces unnecessary antimicrobial pressure while preserving active coverage after cultures, source control, and clinical stability make narrowing coherent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluid resuscitation targets hypoperfusion or shock physiology.
Severe lung injury or overload risk constrains fluid benefit.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema or ARDS risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic bridge while active antimicrobials and source control reshape the causal landscape.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressors are meaningful when hypotension persists despite adequate fluid assessment.

side_effects.interpretation: High vasoconstrictor exposure can worsen ischemic injury when shock is severe.

treatments.context_specific_role: Shock support vector; it improves perfusion while antimicrobial and source-control vectors address the cause.

supportive_care: Treat fever plus severe or expected severe neutropenia as an emergency: rapid triage, vital signs, focused history, complete skin/oral/perianal/line/lung/abdomen exam, and immediate risk assessment.

Obtain CBC with differential, creatinine, liver tests, lactate when ill appearing, CRP/PCT when available, urinalysis when urinary symptoms or catheter context exists, and two blood culture sets before antimicrobials when this does not delay treatment.

Draw blood cultures from each central catheter lumen and peripheral blood when a central line is present; preserve catheter differential time-to-positivity and do not let culture identity replace presentation-time evidence.
Start an antipseudomonal beta-lactam or carbapenem promptly in high-risk or unstable FN while source and resistance context are being clarified.

Reassess at 24-72 hours using fever curve, ANC trajectory, hemodynamics, cultures, source control, organ dysfunction, and imaging; persistent fever is not automatically drug failure but should trigger structured re-evaluation.

Add gram-positive coverage only when context axes support it: catheter infection, skin/soft tissue source, pneumonia, hemodynamic instability, known resistant gram-positive colonization, severe mucositis with viridans concern, or positive gram-positive cultures.

Escalate antifungal evaluation and therapy when fever persists with prolonged/profound neutropenia, pulmonary nodules/halo lesions, candidemia risk, sinus findings, hepatosplenic lesions, prior prophylaxis failure, or clinical deterioration.

Image symptom-directed sources: chest CT for pulmonary symptoms or persistent high-risk fever, abdominal CT/ultrasound for abdominal pain or diarrhea, perianal imaging when pain, swelling, or necrosis is present, and line evaluation for catheter-source suspicion.

For typhlitis: bowel rest, broad gram-negative/anaerobic coverage, serial abdominal exams, surgical consultation for deterioration, perforation, bleeding, necrosis, or uncontrolled sepsis; neutropenia alone is not a reason to ignore surgical source control.

For perianal lesions or ecthyma gangrenosum: inspect early, cover Pseudomonas, obtain wound cultures as confirmatory context, and pursue debridement/drainage/diversion when necrosis or uncontrolled source is present.

Use G-CSF as a host recovery modifier in high-risk or complicated FN contexts, especially expected prolonged/profound neutropenia, pneumonia, shock, invasive fungal disease, or poor marrow recovery; monitor for fever and pulmonary inflammation.

Support shock and organ dysfunction with balanced crystalloids, vasopressors to adequate perfusion, oxygen/ventilation support, kidney replacement therapy for standard indications, glucose control, and careful transfusion support.

Renal- and hepatic-dose adjust antimicrobials; monitor vancomycin exposure, beta-lactam neurotoxicity in renal impairment, aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, amphotericin renal/electrolyte toxicity, azole interactions/QT/hepatotoxicity, and myelosuppressive antivirals.

De-escalate or step down therapy only when pathogen/context, susceptibility, source control, clinical stability, and neutropenia trajectory support it; the narrowing strategy must preserve active coverage.

Distinguish nearby manifolds fairly: AML/APL are defined by blasts, marrow/pathology, DIC/leukostasis patterns; sepsis by organ dysfunction and pathogen/source burden; candidemia by blood culture and deep seeding; PJP by hypoxemic diffuse pneumonia; invasive aspergillosis by nodular/halo/cavitary mold disease. Those confirmatory facts should stay in context/confirmatory sections when structuring cases.
